newsitem.title: FRANCE: INTERVIEW - Saab to remain a niche-player.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Saab to remain a niche-player.

text.p: Swedish carmaker Saab Automobile will remain a niche-player, Saab Chief Executive Robert Hendry said on Monday, but he reiterated the company's goal to reach 150,000 car sales a year.

"Saab Automobile will remain a niche-player, but what our exact size will be in the future I am not sure. I do not know the potential once we reach our goal of selling 150,000 cars a year. It may be 200,000 cars a year, maybe more," Hendry said in an interview with Reuters.
He said the company's goal of reaching sales of 150,000 cars a year by the year 2000 was both feasible and possible.
"I admit that a 50 percent increase in sales in a couple of years is a sizeable challenge," he said.
In 1995, Saab Automobile sold 98,700 cars and the goal for 1996 is 105,000. Saab sold 66,529 cars in the first eight months of 1996, down four percent from January-August 1995 level.
"I do not believe that we will be able to reach 105,000 cars this year, but we will get very close to it," Hendry said.

A key element in making Saab Automobile profitable again is to make the company more customer-oriented and to strengthen the Saab identity as a car for independent thinkers, a car offering high performance, security and intelligent technology.
"We have to turn Saab from being a secret into being known by everybody," Hendry said.
Saab also needs to cut costs further. One way to do that is to increase the number of GM components in future Saab models.

"We can neutralize our small production size by leveraging GM and that, in more ways than one. Components, yes, but also marketing, parts sales and tapping into GM's worldwide organisation. We can do that while still keeping a Saab a Saab," Hendry said.
He does not expect any change in ownership soon. In June, GM and Investor struck an agreement that would allow Investor to sell half of its 50 percent share to GM by the year 2000.
"GM is happy with the present arrangement of 50-50 ownership. There is no pressure from GM to change that," Hendry said.
As Saab nears its sales goal of 150,000 cars a year the company will examine whether its sole plant in Trollhattan, Sweden, will suffice.
"When we get there, an economic decision will be taken as to where we will expand. The plant in Trollhattan will remain without any doubt. It is an important part of our heritage," Hendry added.
